loc_472.loc_102: Antarctic meltwater alters future projections of climate and sea level

loc_465.loc_146: Shaina Sadai 1 , Ambarish V. Karmalkar 2 , David Pollard 3 , Yue Dong 4 , Erica Lucas 5 , Natalya Gomez 5 , Robert DeConto 3 & Alan Condron 6

loc_471.loc_310: Imperfect understanding of ice sheet-climate interactions poses challenges for projecting the impacts of ice sheet mass loss on future climate and sea level. Here we couple a dynamic Antarctic ice sheet model and global climate model to simulate ice sheet-climate interactions. In our single-model, single-member modeling framework, we find sea level and climate projections are significantly modified from uncoupled simulations neglecting Antarctic meltwater under RCP8.5 and RCP4.5. Antarctic meltwater yields surface air temperatures up to 1.5 °C higher in parts of the Northern Hemisphere, while broadly dampening temperature rise in the Southern Hemisphere. Due to radiative feedback changes, both emissions scenarios have global mean surface temperature warming ~0.3 °C lower in the coupled scenario than the control by 2100, with a maximum anomaly of ~1 °C at 2200 under RCP8.5. This slows Antarctica's contribution to global mean sea level rise. Total Antarctic sea level contributions under RCP8.5 (2100: ~0.3m, 2200: >3m) include substantial contributions from East Antarctica, though not under RCP4.5 (2100: ~0.1m, 2200: >1m). Regionally, projected sea level is up to 0.9m higher in the Pacific than the global mean Antarctic contribution under RCP8.5 at 2200.

loc_472.loc_361: The climate system is undergoing unprecedented changes as atmospheric greenhouse gas concentrations continue to rise 1 . The resulting energy imbalance has accelerated ice sheet mass loss and sea level rise, which are projected to continue in coming centuries 2 . Current pledges submitted by parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change are insufficient for meeting the Paris Agreement's Long-Term Temperature Goal of limiting global mean surface temperature (GMST) rise to "well below" 2 °C above pre-industrial values while "pursuing efforts" to limit it to 1.5 °C 3 . These pledges imply a 2.42.6 °C GMST rise by 2100, while current policies imply 2.7 °C warming 4,5 . Insufficient global mitigation risks are locking in large-scale ice sheet mass loss, exposing people and ecosystems around the world to substantial sea level rise. By 2060, over one billion people could be living in low elevation (<10m above sea level) coastal areas, increasing the risks of sea level rise impacts for socially and geographically vulnerable populations 6,7 . Understanding interactions between ice sheets and the broader climate system will be key to constraining future Antarctic ice sheet (AIS) stability, global climate, and sea level 8,9 which in turn has implications for global policy and climate justice 10 .

loc_472.loc_422: Observations confirm that the AIS increasingly contributed to global mean sea level rise (GMSLR) in recent decades 11 , while model projections suggest that the AIS could become the dominant contributor to GMSLR in the coming centuries 2 . Incursions of Antarctic circumpolar deepwater in ice shelf cavities have been implicated as a cause of recent mass loss and grounding line retreat in sectors of East Antarctica 12 . Surface melt is currently observed to various extents across many ice shelves 13 and is expected to become more frequent and longer lasting under medium to high emissions scenarios 14 .

loc_248.loc_158: As the AIS loses mass, meltwater and solid ice enter the Southern Ocean. The current generation of global climate models participating in phases 5 and 6 of the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project (CMIP5 and CMIP6, respectively) lack interactive marine-based ice sheets capable of simulating dynamic ice sheet evolution, such as grounding line retreat, while iteratively coevolving with other climate model components 17 . As a result, CMIP5-6 simulations underestimate ice sheet melt responses under increasing greenhouse gas concentrations, and the impact of meltwater discharge on future climate and sea level 17-19 . In turn, meltwater-induced climate responses impact ice sheet evolution and consequently the timing and magnitude of future GMSLR. The locations of ice sheet mass loss determine the spatial distribution of sea level responses around the world, emphasizing the need to consider gravitational, rotational, and Earth deformation effects on sea level 10,20,21 in addition to climate-ice sheet interactions.

loc_248.loc_273: To assess climatic responses to greenhouse gas forcing and AIS discharge, prior modeling studies have conducted freshwater forcing experiments by adding meltwater to the Southern Ocean 22-26 . Despite variations in the location, quantity, and timing of freshwater input in these studies, modeled responses have several commonalities, including expanded Southern Ocean sea-ice, delayed GMST rise, increased ocean stratification, and subsurface ocean warming around the Antarctic margin. Warmer subsurface ocean temperatures and slowed atmospheric warming impact ice sheet evolution through increased basal melt and delayed surface melt, respectively. To better understand these interactions and more far-field impacts of Antarctic meltwater on the global climate system, dynamic ice sheets should be interactively embedded within global climate models 27 and efforts to achieve this are advancing 28 . Recently, numerical experiments using coupling schemes under climate change projection scenarios have been used to assess climate-ice sheet feedbacks 29,30 and a Southern Ocean meltwater forcing intercomparison project is underway 17 .

loc_248.loc_469: Here, we present results from numerical simulations in which coupling is implemented between the Community Earth System Model (CESM) 1.2, a coupled global climate model which includes interactive atmosphere, ocean, land, and sea-ice modules 31 , and the Penn State University ice sheet model (PSU3D), a dynamic-thermodynamic ice sheet model 32-34 ; (See Methods). We then use a global sea level model that includes 3D viscosity structure 35,36 to understand the spatially variable sea level response resulting from Antarctic mass loss in our coupled ice sheet-climate simulations. Our coupling setup exchanges liquid and solid ice sheet discharge from PSU3D to coastal surface level grid cells in CESM, and passes 2m air temperature, 400m ocean temperature, and precipitation fields from CESM back to PSU3D. CESM does not simulate cavity circulation under floating ice shelves so biascorrected ocean temperatures from CESM are extrapolated under ice shelves in PSU3D. Latent heat from solid ice discharge in PSU3D is accounted for in CESM. Latent heat from liquid melt is accounted for in PSU3D and therefore not reflected in modeled ocean temperatures in CESM. Ice sheet topography in CESM is fixed, while changes in topography evolve in PSU3D. As a result, changes in ice sheet surface height and extent simulated in PSU3D are not felt by the CESM atmosphere or land surface model. Temperature and precipitation values received by PSU3D are lapse rate corrected and surface melt is calculated with a positive degree day scheme, accounting for the partial refreezing of meltwater in the firn layer. Marine ice cliff instability (MICI) dynamics are included (See Methods), providing substantially more meltwater forcing than most previous climate-ice sheet studies. While the validity of MICI remains contested 37 , the intent here is to explore the global impact of meltwater forcing while including brittle ice dynamics which have informed high-end sea level projections.

loc_472.loc_158: We explore changes in climate and sea level under future emissions scenarios RCP4.5 and RCP8.5 from 2005 to 2215. RCP scenarios were used rather than SSPs to make the best use of prior model simulations. RCP4.5 approximately corresponds to SSP2-4.5 and RCP8.5 to SSP5-8.5 38 . While global mitigation efforts should preclude the RCP8.5 scenario in the long-term, we include this scenario because it tracks historical CO2 emissions 39 and provides a useful case study for understanding coupled modeling responses. We include RCP4.5 as it results in end-of-century temperatures that are around or slightly above 2 °C 40 . Within the text, 'coupled' refers to the simulations with interactive coupling between the ice sheet model and climate model and 'control' (or 'uncoupled') refers to the simulations with no interactive AIS which are equivalent to a standard CESM1.2 simulation, which produces minimal meltwater 41 . Due to computational constraints, simulations have one ensemble member per emissions scenario. There is no interactive Greenland Ice Sheet in any simulations presented here as we focus on the Antarctic response. This work builds upon the one-way coupled modeling protocol of Sadai et al. (2020) by implementing interactive coupling.

loc_472.loc_368: In agreement with modern observations (See Methods), we find that from 2005-2020 the West Antarctic Ice Sheet (WAIS) contributes to a sea level rise while the East Antarctic Ice Sheet (EAIS) displays a slight mass gain (Supplementary Fig. 1, Supplementary Table 1). Under RCP8.5, the EAIS begins consistently contributing to sea level rise by 2030, and by 2040 under RCP4.5. Under RCP8.5, the EAIS mass loss increases mainly due to ice shelf melting under a warming atmosphere, leading to an increase in iceberg calving and ice cliff failure at marineterminating ice margins. As a result, the GMSLR contribution from the EAIS surpasses that from the WAIS by 2080 (Supplementary Table 1). By 2100, cumulative GMSLR contributions from West and East Antarctica are similar: 0.15 m from WAIS and 0.19 m from EAIS, producing a total contribution of 0.34m (Fig. 1e, Supplementary Table 1). This is on the upper end of the 0.03-0.34 m range projected for Antarctica in IPCC AR6 under RCP8.5 2 and consistent with uncoupled climateocean-ice sheet simulations that also included ice cliff calving processes 34 . The WAIS contribution by 2100 is dominated by Thwaites Glacier retreating on reverse-sloped bedrock (i.e., from Marine Ice Sheet Instability, MISI, driven retreat) (Fig. 1c). Both Thwaites and Pine Island glaciers are mostly lost in the RCP8.5 simulation by the mid-22 nd century. By 2200, both the Ross and Filchner-Ronne ice shelves collapse, the EAIS margin undergoes widespread mass loss, the Antarctic peninsula thins, and the WAIS retreats (Fig. 1d). Despite the onset of MISI in West Antarctica, the EAIS remains the dominant contributor to GMSLR through the end of the RCP8.5 simulation. The total GMSLR contribution from Antarctica by 2200 is 3.37m, of which 1.75m is sourced from the EAIS and 1.62m from the WAIS (Fig. 1f, Supplementary Table 1).

loc_472.loc_442: Under RCP4.5, lower greenhouse gas forcing limits the AIS GMSLR contribution to 0.13 m by 2100 with 0.1 m from WAIS and 0.03 m from EAIS (Fig. 1e, Supplementary Table 1). The pattern of ice loss mirrors that of RCP8.5 with Thwaites Glacier retreating and Ronne-Filchner thinning, but ice shelf thinning is less extensive overall, particularly in the EAIS (Fig. 1a). By 2200 the AIS GMSLR contribution reaches 1.17m with 0.97m from WAIS and 0.2m from EAIS (Fig. 1f, Supplementary Table 1). The long-term view shows the impact of reducing greenhouse gas forcing; while WAIS still retreats substantially, large sections of the EAIS and portions of the Antarctic peninsula remain intact under RCP4.5 thereby limiting the AIS contribution to GMSLR.

loc_472.loc_402: The impacts of these climatic changes on the ice sheet explain the mass loss and contribution to GMSLR. Increases in SAT drive surface melt and induce hydrofracturing and ice shelf thinning while the accumulated ocean heat (i.e., warming at 400m) increases basal melt under buttressing ice shelves. The concentration of heat in the Ross and Weddell Seas flips cold ice-shelf cavity circulation to warm cavity circulation patterns, accelerating loss of the large ice shelves, triggering MISI and in some places, ice cliff calving.

loc_248.loc_56: Our coupled simulations show that the impacts of AIS discharge into the Southern Ocean are felt globally (Fig. 3). In both RCP4.5 and RCP8.5, freshwater forcing begins suppressing greenhouse gas induced GMST rise by the middle of the 21 st century (Fig. 3c). Under RCP8.5, GMST is 0.33 °C lower by 2100 and 1.05°C lower by 2200 in the coupled simulation than in the control (Fig. 3d; Table 1). Under RCP4.5, GMST in the coupled simulation is 0.29°C lower by 2100 and 0.31°C lower by 2200 than in the control (Fig. 3d, Table 1). Compared to prior uncoupled experiments with the same models 26 , the impact of Antarctic meltwater on GMST is reduced due to the delayed ice sheet mass loss, and, therefore, lower meltwater input, that results from the interactive coupling.

loc_248.loc_205: The delayed GMST warming resulting from Southern Ocean freshwater forcing in our coupled simulations is caused by both a stronger ocean heat uptake efficiency (i.e., more efficient heat storage in the subsurface ocean) and a stronger atmospheric radiative feedback (i.e., more efficient radiative damping at the top of the atmosphere) (ref. 42 ; See Methods). The former is owing to the increased ocean stratification and vertical heat redistribution in the Southern Ocean manifested as subsurface warming (Fig. 2f). The latter is due to the broad surface cooling in both the Southern Ocean and the tropical Pacific driven by freshwater forcing and large-scale teleconnections (Supplementary Fig. 6) 42-44 . The Southern Ocean cooling anomalies and sea-ice expansion locally enhance surface albedo feedback, whereas the tropical East Pacific surface cooling drives a morestabilizing cloud feedback and lapse-rate feedback, resulting from the strengthened tropical west-east zonal sea surface temperature gradient 45,46 . The net radiative feedback parameter over the 21 st century is therefore strengthened from -1.02W/m²/K to -1.13W/m²/K in the coupled RCP8.5 simulation, corresponding to a 0.4°C decrease in effective climate sensitivity (from 3.8°C to 3.4°C) relative to the uncoupled control simulation. The results are qualitatively consistent with the findings in our prior uncoupled freshwater forcing simulations 26,42 .

loc_176.loc_294: Broader Implications of Antarctic Ice Loss

loc_248.loc_469: Antarctic mass loss has important implications for people around the world. Fully understanding the potential impact of Antarctica's contribution to sea level necessitates analyzing the spatial pattern of the sea level response. Global sea level change patterns from ice sheet mass loss are spatially variable due to gravitational, rotational, and Earth deformational (GRD) effects 51 . Using a 3D viscoelastic Earth structure model (See Methods) which includes anomalously low viscosities under the WAIS allows us to account for the sea level impact of water expulsion into the open ocean from formerly ice-covered areas undergoing uplift due to glacial isostatic adjustment 52 . Patterns of sea level change from GRD effects vary spatially and temporally depending on the regions of Antarctic mass loss 21,51 . Consistent with prior research 10,21 we find that regions northward of 30°S will experience sea level rise higher than the Antarctic contribution to GMSLR regardless of emissions scenario and timescales. However, the most heavily impacted regions vary (Fig. 5). Under RCP4.5 by 2100 the Indian, Pacific, and Atlantic Ocean basins, including the Caribbean, experience 0.03m higher regional sea level rise than the global mean (Fig. 5a). By 2200 the pattern is similar but the difference between the highest impacted regions increases by an order of magnitude to 0.3 m (Fig. 5c). Under RCP8.5 by 2100, most of the Pacific basin is projected to experience regional sea level rise of up to 0.09m higher than the GMSLR of 0.34m (Fig. 5b). This pattern remains at 2200 with areas in the central Pacific experiencing 0.9mmore regional sea level rise than the GMSLR of 3.37m while the Indian and Atlantic Ocean basins experience 0.6 and 0.7m higher regional sea levels, respectively

loc_472.loc_293: (Fig. 5d). These regional changes are solely based on the Antarctic response but realized sea level would also depend on Greenland mass loss, thermosteric responses, and other factors which are not accounted for here 21,53 .

loc_472.loc_395: Contrasting the global sea level response to the influence of meltwater on GMST has implications for global mitigation efforts and climate (in)justice 10 . Under RCP8.5, the timing when GMST exceeds 1.5-2°C above preindustrial (defined here following IPCC AR6 as when the 20-year rolling mean exceeds 1.5-2°C above the 1850-1900 average) is minimally affected by the meltwater induced delay in GMST rise (Supplementary Fig. 7a). This is because these warming values are surpassed before the meltwater-induced delayed warming effect strengthens. In our simulations, under high emissions (RCP8.5) 1.5°C is passed by 2026 and 2°C is delayed by 1 year in the coupled simulation. Under RCP4.5, 1.5°C and 2°C are each delayed by 1 year in the coupled simulation (Supplementary Fig. 7b). Given that these are single model runs with one set of models, how meltwater effects and other climate feedbacks impact the timing of different temperature thresholds remains deeply uncertain.

loc_471.loc_469: While the timing of the Long-Term Temperature Goal is minimally impacted, the long-term difference in GMST when accounting for meltwater input and feedbacks is substantial (Table 1) and relevant for informing future global mitigation target setting. The strength of the delayed GMST warming that occurs from Antarctic meltwater forcing should be considered alongside other climate feedbacks, such as the anticipated enhanced warming effect of permafrost melt. The combined impacts of climatic changes that influence GMST with other impacts such as sea level rise could pose substantial challenges if a GMST-based metric was used to inform international policy post2100 10 . In this study we find that GMST is 1.05 °C lower under RCP8.5 by

loc_248.loc_138: 2200 in the coupled simulation compared to the control, but this relatively cooler climate trajectory is commensurate with an Antarctic GMSLR contribution of 3.37 m and regional sea level rise of up to 4.3 m in the Pacific (Fig. 5d). Under RCP4.5, GMST is 0.31°C lower in the coupled simulation by 2200 while Antarctica's contribution to GMSLR is 1.17m and regional sea level rise of up to 1.5m occurs in the Pacific and Indian Ocean basins and Caribbean Sea (Fig. 5c). In other words, while the loss of ice sheet mass results in a slightly lower GMST rise in the coupled simulations, it drives substantial sea level rise. This supports previous work which has argued that focusing on GMST as a metric to inform climate action could exacerbate climate justice concerns 10 . Even with a slower rate of warming, any continued increase in sea level poses risks to island and coastal communities, and raises wide-ranging issues of intergenerational inequity and distributive injustice 10 . The implications for justice and policy are complex and influenced by many other factors that require further detailed study.

loc_248.loc_219: Here we have modeled the impacts of Antarctic ice sheet discharge on climate and sea level using an ice sheet model and climate model in interactive coupling, combined with sea level fingerprint modeling to understand the global patterns of sea level change resulting from ice sheet mass loss. We find that projected rates of future GMST rise are reduced in our coupled simulations under RCP4.5 and RCP8.5 compared to uncoupled simulations. The patterns of meltwater-induced climate effects are not uniform, with reduced future warming over the Southern Ocean and enhanced warming in RCP8.5 over large parts of the Northern Hemisphere, especially by 2100.

loc_248.loc_320: We project a global mean Antarctic contribution to sea level rise of 0.34m by 2100 and 3.37m by 2200 under RCP8.5, with 0.13m by 2100 and 1.17m by 2200 under RCP4.5 (Table 1). Patterns of sea level change are not spatially uniform and more heavily impacted locations vary based on the pattern of ice sheet mass loss. We find that the EAIS contribution to GMSLR over multi-century timescales rivals that of the WAIS and is even slightly higher than that from the WAIS under RCP8.5. Paleoclimate evidence shows signs of past ice sheet retreat in deep EAIS subglacial basins, while future model projections show differing responses. A recent review 54 concluded that the EAIS has the potential to contribute substantially to GMSLR, particularly on multi-century timescales and under high emissions scenarios, as we find here. This also has implications for interpreting sources of sea level rise in the geologic past, which should not assume that the EAIS can only provide a substantial contribution after WAIS has lost all marine-based ice.

loc_472.loc_246: Our study is one of several that have coupled ice sheet models to climate models. Park et al. 29 interactively coupled the same dynamic ice sheet model used in our study (PSU3D) to an intermediate complexity climate model (LOVECLIM), finding that freshwater-induced suppression of atmospheric warming reduced Antarctic mass loss and GMSLR contributions through 2150, in line with our findings using a coupled general circulation model. Siahaan et al. 30 used a different set of coupled models (BISICLES and UKESM) and found Antarctica contributed to a sea level fall by the end of their simulation period in 2100 under RCP8.5 due to increased snowfall exceeding mass loss. The study presented here differs from previous studies by providing a longer term simulation to 2200, including a radiative feedback analysis which allows for an assessment of the mechanisms behind delayed GMST rise, and offline coupling to a sea level model which allows for an assessment of the global sea level fingerprint that results from AIS mass loss. By including an ice sheet model that simulates hydrofracturing and ice-cliff calving, ice loss in our simulations is highly sensitive to evolving atmospheric conditions. This also tests the climate impacts and feedbacks resulting from a large meltwater flux to the Southern Ocean. More generally, our study complements previous work by assessing divergent climate-sea level responses of different sets of coupled models, highlighting the need to include dynamic ice sheets in more global climate models.

loc_472.loc_287: The results presented here demonstrate the importance of embedding dynamic ice sheet models within Earth system models used for future climate, ice sheet, and sea level projections. They also highlight the global risks of Antarctic ice sheet instability under rising greenhouse gas emissions, underscoring the need to reduce emissions in the immediate near-term.

loc_472.loc_388: The climate model used is Community Earth System Model 1.2.2 with Community Atmospheric Model 5 atmospheric physics (CESM1CAM5) 31 . CESM1.2 is a coupled global Earth system model containing interactive ocean, atmosphere, sea-ice, and land models linked via a coupler. The continent and ocean boundaries do not change in CESM1.2. CESM1.2 does not include fully interactive Greenland or Antarctic ice sheets 58 . It was run with 1° resolution for the ocean and sea-ice components and 0.9×1.25° resolution for the atmosphere and land components. The model grid has a displaced pole over Greenland. It is initialized with 20 th century restart files. Simulations spanning the period from 2005-2200 and were conducted under Representative Concentration Pathway RCP8.5 and RCP4.5 59 .

loc_472.loc_469: The Antarctic ice sheet model used is the Penn State University ice sheet model (PSU3D) 32,33 . PSU3D is a three-dimensional ice sheet model that approximates ice flow using hybrid ice dynamics with an imposed parameterization of ice flux across the grounding line 60 , allowing for realistic simulation of grounding line retreat 32 . In these simulations it is run at a 10 km resolution with basal sliding coefficients obtained from an inverse run matching modeled surface elevations and observations 61 . Initial conditions were from DeConto et al. 34 , which included simulations using offline CESM1.2 forcing. Bed topographic boundary conditions use Bedmap2 62 . We use CESM1.2 and PSU3D with Bedmap2 boundary conditions to make the best use of previously run control experiments.

loc_248.loc_84: Models were run on the NCAR Cheyenne high performance computing system 63 . For the control scenarios, there is no freshwater forcing provided by the PSU3D ice sheet model. Testing determined that our RCP8.5 control matched the SAT evolution of the standard CMIP5 CESM1 simulation for RCP8.5, which is used for the time series in Fig. 3 64 . For RCP4.5, data from CESM1-CAM5_rcp45_r1i1p1 obtained from the CMIP5 data repository was used as a control 65 . Preindustrial temperature data was obtained from the CMIP5 data repository 66 .

loc_248.loc_354: CESM1.2 and PSU3D are run with an annual interactive coupling scheme allowing for a dynamic response of the ice sheet to changes in the climate model, and response of the climate system to ice sheet freshwater discharge. The annual coupling is accomplished as follows 67 . An initial climatology is used to force PSU3D for one model year (2005), provided from a standard CESM1.2 control simulation lacking additional meltwater forcing. The ice sheet model is then run for one model year to provide liquid water and solid ice discharge from the ice sheet, interpolated onto the CESM1.2 ocean grid at the nearest coastal ocean cell from where the mass loss occurs in the ice sheet. Latent heat is accounted for as solid ice melts. The ice sheet model internally determines which types of ice sheet discharge exit as a solid or liquid. Latent heat of the solid ice discharge phase change is accounted for in the climate model while latent heat for liquid fields is accounted for within the ice sheet model 32 . Latent heat from fields the ice sheet counts as liquid is accounted for within the ice sheet model. This may underestimate the delayed warming effect of ice sheet discharge on global climate; therefore, the extent of the delayed warming effect seen in this study should be taken as a lower bound. The fields the ice sheet model outputs as liquid melt components include ice sheet basal melt, sub-ocean ice face melt, percolation of meltwater to the base, and the counter effect of basal refreezing while the solid ice discharge forcing contains ice lost from calving and cliff failure. Liquid and solid discharge components enter the climate model at the surface ocean level 55,68 . While injecting freshwater at depth can lead to more mixing and a deeper mixed layer and work with other ocean models has shown the depth of freshwater input to have an effect in other models 69 , previous work with CESM indicates that there is little difference in CESM1-simulated ocean surface temperature, salinity, and sea-ice responses when freshwater is applied at depth versus in experiments where freshwater is added at the surface 41 . Following the calculation of interpolated liquid and solid ice sheet discharge, CESM1.2 is then run for one model year to obtain a meltwaterperturbed climatology. Ocean temperature at 400m depth, 2m surface air temperatures, and precipitation are then passed back to the ice sheet. The ice sheet model is built to intake ocean temperatures at 400m as this depth level is representative of where warm deep water enters the Amundsen Sea Embayment 70,71 .

loc_248.loc_436: Initial surface topography is provided to the climate sheet model by the ice sheet model at the first time step. At subsequent time steps, deviations between the input topography and evolving ice sheet topography are accommodated via lapse rate corrections for temperature and precipitation 70 . The fraction of input precipitation that falls as snow versus rain is parameterized based on the input surface air temperature. The ice sheet model surface mass balance calculations account for surface melting and refreezing as well as percolation of liquid water below the ice sheet surface layer. Surface melt is calculated via a positive degree day scheme, which calculates melt from the input temperature and precipitation, with melt beginning at -1°C based on observational relationships 72 .

loc_472.loc_409: As used here, the ice sheet model accounts for enhanced calving at thick (O 1000m) marine-terminating ice fronts that have lost their buttressing ice shelves, leaving tall subaerial ice cliffs prone to brittle failure 76 . We adopt the finite volume sea level solver to solve the sea level equation on a global tetrahedral grid including 3D variations in Earth's rheological structure 35 . The grid is regionally refined in Antarctica, with a resolution of 6 km to the base of the MOHO, 12 km to 220 km depth, and 25 km to 350 km depth 36 .
